prompt: In the lesson's model, which cost of an automated check is paid once rather than again and again?

choices.text: Writing it
choices.why: Right. Maintenance, runs and false alarms keep arriving for as long as the test stays in the suite.

choices.text: Maintaining it when the application changes
choices.why: That one recurs: every change that breaks the test and not the product is paid again.

choices.text: The seconds each run takes on the machine
choices.why: Those are multiplied by the number of runs, which is thousands a year in the lesson's assumption.

choices.text: Investigating a red run that turns out to be nothing at all
choices.why: Each false alarm costs a person's minutes again; lesson 14's flaky tests are where they pile up.

prompt: In the experiment, the screenshot test went red on the darker border and on the new banana price. Where do those two runs go in the model?

choices.text: Value: two defects caught before a customer saw them
choices.why: Neither was a defect; both were changes somebody meant, so nothing was caught.

choices.text: Nowhere, because updating a baseline costs nothing
choices.why: The command is quick; deciding that the new picture is right is a person's minutes, every time.

choices.text: Maintenance, in a person's minutes
choices.why: Right. At one change of look a week that line alone was 500 minutes a year.

choices.text: Machine time, kept in its own column
choices.why: The runs took under a second each; what costs is the person who has to read them.

prompt: Keep the lesson's assumptions for the screenshot test (10 minutes to write, 10 minutes for each change that breaks it), but say the shop's look changes twice a month. What is its person cost for a year?
hint: Twelve months, two changes each, plus the writing.

prompt: The lesson says the sideways check is cheap for a reason that does not depend on its assumptions. Which reason?

choices.text: It runs in under half a second
choices.why: Run time is machine time, a column of its own; a slow check with one right answer would still need no maintenance.

choices.text: Its question has one right answer at every width
choices.why: Right. The border, the price and the white prices all left it green; only the width it asks about moves it.

choices.text: It is marked with test.fail(), so a failure does not count
choices.why: The mark covers two widths and one known defect; it is not why harmless edits leave the check green.

choices.text: It was written by lesson 7, before the shop's look began changing
choices.why: When it was written does not matter; the four edits came after it, and it stayed green on the harmless three.

prompt: Match each case with what the lesson does instead of a browser test.

pairs.left: A CAPTCHA on the sign-up form
pairs.right: Turned off in the test environment, or the provider's test keys
The provider's sandbox and its test cards

pairs.left: A feature nobody has seen yet

pairs.right: A unit or API test, a layer below

prompt: A test fills in the sign-up form and gets past its CAPTCHA on every run. What has it shown?

choices.text: That sign-up is now covered from end to end
choices.why: It covered sign-up by beating the one part meant to stop it, which is a finding about that part.

choices.text: That the CAPTCHA does not stop a program, which is a defect to report
choices.why: Right. A CAPTCHA exists so that a program cannot pass it; this one was passed.

choices.text: That the CAPTCHA works, since the form still accepted the visitor
choices.why: The visitor was a program; accepting it is the opposite of working.

choices.text: Nothing, since a CAPTCHA is outside the shop's own code
choices.why: Whose code it is decides who fixes it, not whether the finding counts.

prompt: The shop adds a delivery map from another company. The browser test that drives the map fails on the day that company releases. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Retries, until their release has settled
choices.why: A retry turns their change into a flake you have stopped seeing; lesson 14 says what that costs.

choices.text: Stub the map and test your side, failures included
choices.why: Right. Your request and your handling of each answer, a refusal and a timeout among them, are yours to test.

choices.text: Remove every test of the page that shows the map, since it is theirs
choices.why: The rest of the page is still yours, and so is what it sends to the map.

choices.text: Pin the version of their page the tests see
choices.why: Their page is served by them; your suite has no way to choose its version.

prompt: A test has passed on every run for a year. What does the lesson say to do before deciding its fate?

choices.text: Delete it: a year of green means there is nothing left for it to catch
choices.why: Green can mean the thing it guards never broke, and it may be guarded because it matters.

choices.text: Mark it with test.fail() until it fails once
choices.why: That turns a working test into one that reports a pass as a failure, which is backwards.

choices.text: Break what it guards on purpose and see whether it goes red
choices.why: Right. A test that can still fail is guarding something; one that cannot is the useless kind.

choices.text: Leave it alone, since a test that passes costs nothing
choices.why: It still costs its runs, and its maintenance when the page changes.

prompt: Why does the lesson call a flaky test that nobody fixes worse than no test?

choices.text: Because it slows the suite down with retries
choices.why: Slowness is a cost, but not the one that makes it worse than nothing.

choices.text: Because red runs get rerun, the real ones too
choices.why: Right. Red stops meaning anything, for every test in the suite and not only for that one.

choices.text: Because Playwright refuses to run a suite with one
choices.why: It runs it; lesson 14's `--fail-on-flaky-tests` is a choice, not a default.

choices.text: Because it hides a defect in the application
choices.why: Often the cause is in the test; the damage is to what a red run means.

prompt: Put in order what happens to a test marked with test.fail() once the defect it documents is fixed.
items: Playwright reports *Expected to fail, but passed* and the suite is red
The test guards the fix from then on

prompt: A test marked with `test.fail()` is reported as passing on ___ failure, which is why the lesson prints the error each one had.
Why was the run that measures the suite made with `--workers 1`?

choices.text: Because the JSON reporter only works with one worker
choices.why: It works with any number; the five runs after it used the default.

choices.text: Because one worker is faster
choices.why: It is slower; the point was a measurement that other tests could not muddle.

choices.text: Because tests share one basket
choices.why: Right. Lessons 15 and 19 are about that basket; one worker keeps it out of the numbers.

choices.text: Because test.fail() needs a single worker to report correctly
choices.why: An expected failure is reported the same way with any number of workers.

prompt: A suite of 80 tests runs 10 times with no change to the code. Three runs are red, each time with one test that passes when run alone. Which number does the lesson track?

choices.text: 3 red runs in 10, 30% of the suite's runs
choices.why: Right. A person meets a red run, not a red test, so the share of runs is what they live with.

choices.text: 3 failures in 800 test runs, under half a percent
choices.why: True arithmetic, and it makes the suite look healthy while three days in ten start with a red run.

choices.text: The number of retries needed to make each run green
choices.why: Retries hide the rate rather than measure it; lesson 14 shows them turning failures into *flaky*.

choices.text: The run time of the slowest test file
choices.why: That is the budget's number, a different one; it says nothing about red runs.

prompt: A test marked with `test.fail()` waits its whole 5-second timeout before it fails, as it should. The suite runs 5,000 times a year. How many minutes of machine time does that one test spend a year?
hint: Seconds times runs, then divide by 60.

prompt: Which course comes next in the qa track, after this one?

choices.text: `api-mobile-automation`
choices.why: Right. It goes a layer down, to the API, before it turns to mobile.

choices.text: `non-functional-testing`
choices.why: It builds on this course, and comes after `api-mobile-automation` in the track.

choices.text: `manual-testing`
choices.why: That one comes before: this course assumes it.

choices.text: `testing-cicd`
choices.why: It is in the track, later, where the suite moves into a pipeline.

prompt: The white prices of the experiment passed every check in this course's project. Which course tests the fact that would have caught them?

choices.text: `api-mobile-automation`, since the price comes from the API
choices.why: The API sent the right price; the defect was in how the page drew it.

choices.text: `manual-testing`, since only a person can see a colour
choices.why: A person would see it, but contrast has a right answer, which a check can measure.

choices.text: `testing-cicd`, by running the screenshot on every push
choices.why: Running it more often adds to its maintenance and asks the same question about pixels.

choices.text: `non-functional-testing`, in its lessons on accessibility
choices.why: Right. White on white is a contrast failure, and lessons 12 to 15 there test contrast.

prompt: A screenshot test catches about one defect a year, worth 465 minutes. It is red on 60 harmless changes a year, at 10 minutes each. What does the lesson suggest first?

choices.text: Retries, so harmless changes stop turning the suite red
choices.why: A changed page differs on every try, so a retry fails again.

choices.text: Update the baseline automatically whenever it fails
choices.why: Then it accepts every picture, the defect's included, and catches nothing.

choices.text: Narrow it, or ask for the fact under the picture
choices.why: Right. 610 minutes against 465 is a loss, and narrowing cuts the cost without losing the defect.

choices.text: Nothing, since one caught defect justifies any test
choices.why: The model compares the two numbers, and here the cost is the larger one.

prompt: A test marked with `test.fail()` for a defect in the search page has passed for months. `slowest.mjs` now prints its error as `page.goto: net::ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED`. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The defect is still there, since the test still fails
choices.why: It fails before it reaches the search box, so it says nothing about the defect.

choices.text: It fails for another reason, not the defect
choices.why: Right. `test.fail()` accepts any failure; the error is how you see which one it got.

choices.text: The defect was fixed and the mark should be removed
choices.why: A fixed defect makes the test pass, and Playwright then reports *Expected to fail, but passed*.

choices.text: The test is flaky and belongs in quarantine
choices.why: Nothing says it varies between runs; it fails the same way every time, for the wrong reason.

prompt: Which of these makes a case a good candidate for a browser test, in the lesson's terms?

choices.text: Frequent, stable, comparable by a machine, costly when broken
choices.why: Right. The basket total and the sideways scroll are both like that.

choices.text: It is on the manual test list and nobody has automated it yet
choices.why: The list is not a backlog: some cases on it should never move.

choices.text: It is about a feature nobody has explored yet
choices.why: A test written now freezes a guess; explore first.

choices.text: It needs somebody to judge whether the copy reads well
choices.why: A judgement has no answer a machine can compare.

prompt: Before deleting a test, what does the lesson ask you to write down?

choices.text: Nothing: the history of the repository keeps the file and its author
choices.why: It keeps the code and not the reason; the next person sees a missing test and no why.

choices.text: The number of times it passed before it was removed
choices.why: Passing says little on its own; what it checked and what covers it now say more.

choices.text: What it checked, why it goes, and what covers that risk now
choices.why: Right. That turns a deletion into a decision somebody can disagree with later.

choices.text: Who wrote the test originally, so they can be asked about it
choices.why: The author is in the history already; the reason is not.
